text: A heavy iron door or lid makes a loud metallic clang when it is shut.
exceptions: A door closed gently or on good hinges may make little noise.

text: A saucer of milk set down in a house is usually meant for a small animal.
exceptions: It may be left over from a person's own use, or set out for some other purpose.

text: Popular belief in the period held that snakes will drink milk.
exceptions: A folk belief, not established natural history.

text: India has many venomous snakes, whose bite leaves only small punctures and can kill quickly.
exceptions: Many snakes are harmless, and the speed of death varies with species and dose.

text: Animals can be taught to come to a particular sound, especially when it is followed by food.
exceptions: Some animals train poorly, and none responds every time.

text: People stand on chairs to reach things high on a wall, and shoes can leave marks on the seat.
exceptions: A marked seat can have other causes, and a clean shoe may leave nothing visible.

reads: a large iron safe
text: Roylott's bare room contains a large iron safe.

reads: a small wooden shelf full of books, mostly of a technical character
text: A recluse with a shelf of technical books is still working at something. We are not told the subject, though medicine is the natural guess.
Here is a candidate for the clang. An iron safe in the next room could make a sound 'as if a mass of metal had fallen' (¶50) if its door were shut hard.
hindsight: The safe is only listed with the furniture. A first-time reader must carry the clang forward from ¶50 and be looking for a metal object.

reads: were the principal things which met the eye
text: Nothing on this list could make or send a gas: no jar, pipe or apparatus. Watson gives only the principal things, so it is not conclusive, but the gas idea gets no help here.

reads: What’s in here?
text: Of everything in the room, the safe gets his first question.

reads: My stepfather’s business papers.
text: Helen says the safe holds Roylott's business papers.

reads: Only once, some years ago.
text: Her 'business papers' rests on one look years ago. She was also wrong about where the bell-rope went. She cannot say what is in the safe now.

reads: There isn’t a cat in it, for example?
text: An absurd question to ask about a safe, but Holmes is not idling. He is asking whether something alive could be kept in there.

reads: a small saucer of milk which stood on the top of it
text: A saucer of milk stands on top of the safe.
So the cat question came from a saucer he had already seen. Milk in a saucer suggests that some small animal is being fed in this room.
The milk is on the very safe he asked about. What is fed here and what is locked up here may be the same thing, odd as it seems to keep a living creature in an iron box.

reads: No; we don’t keep a cat.
text: The household has no cat, as far as Helen knows.

reads: But there is a cheetah and a baboon.
text: Helen's own answer: the milk may be for one of the animals we know about.
options: It is for some animal she does not know about

reads: a saucer of milk does not go very far in satisfying its wants
text: Holmes disposes of the cheetah, and the baboon is just as much a creature of the grounds. A small saucer in the bedroom points to something smaller, which Helen has not mentioned.

Something small may be fed in a room joined to the death room by a little opening, and its owner receives Indian animals from abroad. The 'small living thing' on my list looks more possible. What sort of thing?
options: A small mammal, cat-sized or less
A snake or other long, thin Indian creature, which could go down a rope and might be what Julia called a band
No creature: the milk is his own, or carries a drug
hindsight: The text names no such creature. A first-time reader must join the milk, the Indian animals of ¶27, the rope and the word 'band' unaided, and the snake option also needs the folk belief about milk.

text: A living thing would cover what gas could not. The rope gives it a road to the pillow, the whistle could be a call, and the nights Julia heard the whistle unharmed could be nights when it did nothing. The doctors finding no poison and no marks still has to be explained.
hindsight: This is the reader's own synthesis. Nothing in the text yet connects the whistle with the milk.

reads: He squatted down in front of the wooden chair and examined the seat of it with the greatest attention.
text: Holmes closely inspects the seat of the plain wooden chair.

reads: That is quite settled
text: Settled how? He does not say what the seat showed, or why the plain chair matters when the armchair is the one beside the bed.
options: The seat shows someone has stood on it
The seat shows something else was rested on it

text: On Julia's side the hook is above the opening, and the rope hangs down from there to the bed, so the ventilator is some way up the wall. If Roylott uses it from this side, he may need to stand on something, and the plain chair against the wall would do.
options: He stands on the chair to reach the ventilator
He stands on it to reach something else
hindsight: We are told neither the height of the opening on this side nor what the seat showed.

reads: a small dog lash hung on one corner of the bed
text: A small dog lash hangs on the corner of Roylott's bed.

reads: curled upon itself and tied so as to make a loop of whipcord
text: The lash has been tied into a loop.
Nobody has mentioned a dog. We hear of a cheetah and a baboon, so what is a dog lash doing by his bed?

A whip tied so that it cannot be used as a whip has been made into something else. A noose seems the likeliest, but for what? It is unlikely to have been used on Julia, who had no marks of violence (¶56).
options: A loop for catching or handling a small creature at arm's length
A tool for working something at the ventilator or the safe
Nothing to do with the crime
hindsight: Nothing says what the loop is for. The handling option is attractive only to a reader already thinking of a creature.

reads: I think that I have seen enough now
text: Saucer, chair and looped lash, and then he has seen enough. Those are what he reacted to in this room, so his answer probably runs through them.

reads: when a clever man turns his brains to crime it is the worst of all
text: Holmes now speaks of crime and of a clever man, straight after searching Roylott's room. He means the doctor, and he has stopped treating him as a mere brute.
Nobody reports the ventilator's other end in this room. I expect it is here, but neither Holmes nor Watson has said so.

reads: I had never seen my friend’s face so grim or his brow so dark
text: He joked when Roylott bent the poker. What he has just seen disturbs him far more.

reads: Your life may depend upon your compliance.
text: He ties her survival to what happens next, so he thinks a further attempt may be very close.

reads: both my friend and I must spend the night in your room
text: Holmes and Watson are to spend the night in the middle room.
The tooth-brush guess holds: he meant to stay the night, and in the house itself.

reads: Your windows would be visible from there?
text: The Crown, opposite the house, will be their waiting place, with a view of her window.
The Crown supplied Helen's dog-cart, so it is one place Roylott may have asked about her. Waiting there risks talk, and Holmes accepts that for the sake of the view.

reads: put your lamp there as a signal to us
text: Her lamp in the window will be the signal to come.

reads: withdraw quietly with everything which you are likely to want into the room which you used to occupy
text: Helen is to move secretly back to her old room for the night.

reads: on pretence of a headache
text: The headache keeps her from facing a man who knows she went to Holmes, and it gives him reason to believe she is shut in the middle room for the evening.
The middle room is to seem occupied by her while she is elsewhere. That probably answers why he has not sent her to Harrow: with her openly gone, nothing would happen tonight.
He moves her only one room along, to a room with a pierced wall on the same corridor. So what he fears belongs to the middle room and is not a man walking the house.

reads: you must open the shutters of your window, undo the hasp
text: The window he could not force will be their way in, opened from inside. They avoid the corridor that passes Roylott's door, and she acts only after he has retired, so he will not see it done.

reads: we shall investigate the cause of this noise which has disturbed you
text: 'This noise' is a mild phrase from a man who has just said her life may depend on this and who had Watson bring a revolver. He is telling her less than he thinks.

With Roylott next door and the room apparently holding Helen, the whistle should come in the small hours, about three as Julia said (¶40), and whatever uses the opening should come with it. Holmes and Watson will be there to meet it.

reads: Perhaps I have.
text: He as good as admits that he has a solution, and he keeps it to himself.

reads: I should prefer to have clearer proofs before I speak.
text: By his own account he lacks proof. What he has is inference from fittings, a saucer, a chair and a loop of cord, and tonight is the test of it.

reads: I think that there was probably some more tangible cause.
text: Holmes rejects Helen's belief that Julia died of pure fright (¶60). Something physical reached her, though this is only his opinion and he says 'probably'.
I will let gas go. Nothing listed in the room could produce it, it has no need of a rope, it explains neither whistle nor clang, and Holmes's interest went to milk, a chair and a loop of whipcord.

reads: if Dr. Roylott returned and saw us our journey would be in vain
text: Roylott knows Helen consulted Holmes but must not know of this visit. The plan needs him to behave as usual tonight, so Holmes is in effect waiting for the attempt to be made.

Open: what came through the ventilator, what the 'speckled band' was, what the rope, milk, chair seat and looped lash each mean, what is really in the safe, what whistles and what clanged, what the other 'little changes' were, how Roylott traced Helen, and what his business in town is.

Working picture: Roylott, clever as well as brutal, built the false ventilator and rope to reach the bed in the middle room. The milk, chair and loop suggest he may keep something small in his room and send it through, though Holmes has confirmed nothing. Tonight the room is a trap, with Helen one door along. She probably survives, and Roylott's advertised death may come out of this night.
options: A small creature sent through the opening and down the rope
A poison or drug delivered through the opening by some means using the milk or cord
Something else that has not yet been thought of
hindsight: The creature option depends on the reader's own joining of ¶27 with the milk and the rope. Holmes has said only that the cause is 'more tangible' than fright.
